## Introduction
- First series of laparoscopic colectomies reported in 1991.
- Included laparoscopic right hemicolectomies and sigmoid resections.
- Initial studies supported laparoscopy as safe and feasible.
- Operative times and inpatient length of stay comparable to recent studies.

## Initial Concerns and Adoption
- Adoption of laparoscopy in colorectal surgery slowly increased.
- Initially not universally accepted.
- Concerns centered around cost and feasibility.
- Lack of high-quality evidence supporting it over open surgery.

## Early Oncologic Concerns
- Concerns about trocar-related bowel injuries.
- Oncologic safety questioned due to high rates of trocar site recurrences.
- Early review reported 35 cases of port site recurrences over 3 years.
- Led to significant caution in utilizing laparoscopy for cancer.

## Landmark Randomized Trials
- High-quality RCTs alleviated early concerns:
  - COST (Clinical Outcomes of Surgical Therapy)
  - COLOR (Colon Cancer Laparoscopic or Open Resection)
  - CLASICC (Conventional versus Laparoscopic-Assisted Surgery)
- Demonstrated no difference in oncologic outcomes between laparoscopic and open procedures.

## Benefits Established by Trials
- Reduced Length of Stay (LOS).
- Earlier return of bowel function.
- Reduced pain and narcotic usage.
- National database analyses confirmed decreased ICU stay, overall LOS, complications, blood transfusions, and readmission rates.

## The Learning Curve
- Complex laparoscopy involves a steep learning curve.
- Tekkis et al. modeled data from over 900 patients.
- Concluded 55 right-sided and 62 left-sided resections required to overcome the learning curve.
- Structured colorectal training programs help surgeons overcome this quickly.

## Introduction to Robotic Surgery
- Robotics advanced minimally invasive colorectal techniques.
- Generally considered an extension of laparoscopy.
- Perceived benefits:
  - Advanced optics (stereoscopic vision, image magnification).
  - Improved dexterity (ergonomic hand controls).
  - Tremor reduction.

## Robotic Surgery Advantages
- Offers potential to overcome conventional laparoscopy difficulties:
  - Intracorporeal suturing.
  - Operating in obese patients.
  - Challenging anatomical sites (e.g., the pelvis).
- Uptake has been swift in many parts of the world.

## Robotic Surgery Limitations
- High-quality evidence supporting its use over conventional laparoscopy is still lacking.
- Issues surrounding cost and sustainability limit utilization.
- Some studies highlight increased rates of iatrogenic complications compared to conventional laparoscopy.

## Robotic Learning Curve
- Noted learning curve associated with robotics.
- Approximately 75 cases required to gain proficiency when establishing a program.
- Reduces to 25 to 30 cases once an established robotics program is in place.

## Short-Term Outcomes: Operative Time
- Laparoscopic procedures have longer operative times than open (30 to 84 minutes difference).
- Robotic operations show an additional increase in operative times compared to laparoscopic (32 to 127 minutes).

## Short-Term Outcomes: Conversion Rates
- Conversion rates for laparoscopy vary across studies (3 percent to 25 percent).
- CLASICC study reported highest conversion (25 percent), but it decreased over the study (learning curve effect).
- Comparison between laparoscopic and robotic mostly showed no difference, except some studies showed significantly lower conversion with robotics.

## Short-Term Outcomes: Length of Stay
- Universal advantage of laparoscopy is decreased LOS.
- Difference ranges from 1 day (COST) to 5 days (Liang et al.).
- Basse et al. showed 2-day LOS in both groups with a universal fast-track protocol.
- Raises question if laparoscopy advantages are blunted by Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols.

## Short-Term Outcomes: Morbidity and Mortality
- Majority of studies found no significant differences in short-term morbidity and mortality between laparoscopic, robotic, and open groups.
- Some studies demonstrated lower overall postoperative complications in laparoscopic versus open, driven by lower wound infection rates.
- Robotic and laparoscopic approaches show significantly lower complication rates compared to open.

## Short-Term Outcomes: Lymph Node Harvest
- Lymph node harvest is a surrogate marker for oncologic quality.
- Most studies show no difference in the number of lymph nodes harvested among approaches.
- Lim et al. showed lower nodes with robotic for low anterior resections, but average still meets AJCC and UICC minimum recommendations.
- Laparoscopic and robotic approaches afford higher odds of harvesting 12 or more nodes compared to open.

## Return of Bowel Function
- Consistent earlier return of bowel function in laparoscopic versus open.
- Hypothesized to result from gentler tissue handling and decreased LOS.
- Basse et al. found no difference with fast-track protocols, supporting the hypothesis that laparoscopy benefit relates to shortened ileus.
- Robotic versus laparoscopic: differences range from no difference to 1.5 days in favor of robotics (overcoming ICA challenges).

## Postoperative Pain
- Measured differently across trials.
- Most studies used narcotic usage as a surrogate.
- Found reduced narcotic usage in laparoscopic versus open.
- Highly beneficial given increasing pressure to decrease opiate prescriptions.
- Park et al. found no differences in visual analog pain scores between laparoscopic and robotic right colectomies.

## Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)
- ERAS programs established to reduce perioperative complications and LOS.
- First colorectal-specific ERAS guidelines published in 2005.
- 2011 Cochrane review showed significant reduction in LOS and overall complications.
- Updated to 4th edition in 2019, including recommendations for minimally invasive approaches.

## ERAS and Same-Day Discharge
- ERAS protocols implemented at multiple institutions, reducing LOS.
- Studies report feasibility of same-day discharge following colectomies in well-selected patients.
- McLemore et al. review: 62 percent to 93 percent of patients discharged same day.
- 30-day readmission 0.8 percent to 6 percent; anastomotic leak and reoperation rates remained low.

## Costs: Laparoscopic versus Open
- Cost of operation is higher for laparoscopic colectomy.
- Driven by increased equipment and disposable instrument costs.
- COLOR group reported higher operation, admission, and healthcare system costs.
- However, total cost to society (including time off work) showed no difference at 12 months.

## Costs: Robotic versus Laparoscopic
- Robotic approach has consistently higher costs for the operation itself.
- High cost of da Vinci system (up to 2.5 million dollars) is a driving factor.
- Often offset by decreased LOS, conversion, and complications, resulting in equivalent overall costs.
- Conversion to open significantly increases costs, making reduction in conversion rate a driver in lowering overall cost.

## Long-Term Oncologic Outcomes
- Key motivating factor: demonstrate equivalent oncologic outcomes.
- Trials published updates out to 10 years.
- No significant difference in overall survival, disease-free survival, wound recurrence, or overall recurrence between laparoscopic and open.
- Laparoscopic colectomy is noninferior to open in appropriately selected cancer patients.

## Long-Term Outcomes: Robotic versus Laparoscopic
- Few studies examine long-term oncologic outcomes for robotics.
- Lim et al. found no differences in overall or disease-free survival between laparoscopic and robotic for sigmoid resection.
- Yuval et al. found no difference in survival among laparoscopic, robotic, or open approaches.
- Minimally invasive approaches associated with fewer complications and shorter LOS.

## Incisional Hernia and Adhesive SBO
- Hypothesized that smaller incisions in laparoscopy would decrease risk of these complications.
- Literature is mixed; majority found no difference.
- LAFA study showed decreases in both outcomes in the laparoscopic group.
- Robotic surgery: increased rates of intracorporeal anastomosis (ICA) lead to off-midline extraction sites, potentially leading to fewer incisional hernias.

## Quality of Life (QoL)
- Challenging outcome to compare due to numerous instruments.
- Most trials found at least some short-term QoL benefit in the laparoscopic group.
- COST group found slightly better global QoL at 2 weeks and 18 months.
- Braga et al. found significantly better general health and functioning at 12 months, but difference disappeared at 48 months.
- Differences most significant in the first 6 to 12 months.

## Robotic Surgery: Environmental Sustainability
- Sustainability in surgery is a strong focus (reduce emissions and waste).
- Up to 10 percent of carbon emissions arise from healthcare.
- Papadopoulou et al. demonstrated robotically assisted surgery is associated with significantly more solid waste and increased greenhouse gases compared to laparoscopy, despite reusable equipment.

## Intracorporeal versus Extracorporeal Anastomosis
- Extracorporeal anastomosis (ECA) is common for laparoscopic right hemicolectomy.
- Requires upper midline incision; challenging in obese patients.
- Intracorporeal anastomosis (ICA) requires less mobilization and traction.
- Suprapubic extraction site can be utilized with ICA, reducing pain and hernia risk.
- Robotic platform makes ICA easier due to articulating instruments.

## ICA versus ECA: Clinical Evidence
- Retrospective studies largely found no significant differences in operative time, complications, or LOS.
- Prospective series and RCTs found ICA associated with quicker return of bowel function and reduced pain and wound complications.
- However, this did not consistently translate into a shorter LOS.
- Either ECA or ICA are acceptable approaches based on surgeon training.

## Complete Mesocolic Excision (CME)
- Popularized since 2009.
- Based on sharp dissection along embryological planes.
- Ensures entire mesocolon and lymph nodes removed as a complete package.
- Vasculature ligated at its origin (Central Vascular Ligation).
- Believed to be oncologically superior due to extensive lymphadenectomy.

## CME with CVL: Evidence
- Retrospective and population-based studies reported decreased recurrence and cancer mortality.
- Meta-analyses show greater lymph node yield without increased morbidity.
- RCTs show CME is feasible, increases lymph node yield, but vascular complications may be more common.
- Currently, no definitive oncologic survival benefit proven in RCTs for right or left colon cancer.

## Single Incision Laparoscopic Colectomy (SILC)
- Increases complexity, goal is limiting incision to specimen extraction only.
- Early case reports established feasibility for cancer and IBD.
- Two RCTs comparing SILC with standard laparoscopy showed similar operating times, complication rates, and lymph node harvests.
- Decreased LOS by 1 day in one study.
- Promising technique for appropriately selected patients.

## Techniques: Right Colectomy - Positioning
- Patient placed in supine position.
- Laparoscopic: left arm tucked.
- Robotic: both arms tucked.
- Placed on nonsliding mat, secured with straps.
- Modified lithotomy or split-leg if tumor location unclear, to facilitate intraoperative endoscopy.
- Slight Trendelenburg with table inclined toward the left.

## Techniques: Right Colectomy - Port Placement
- Abdomen entered midline (Hasson) or LUQ (Veress).
- Pneumoperitoneum established.
- Thorough evaluation of abdomen for disseminated disease and R0 feasibility.
- Reference to Figure 182.1 for 4-port laparoscopic and 4-arm robotic configurations.

## Right Colectomy: Medial-to-Lateral Approach
- Omentum retracted superiorly; small bowel moved to left side.
- Grasping cecum or mesentery highlights ileocolic artery branching from SMA.
- Creates a tenting or bowstringing effect.
- Opening in peritoneum parallel to ileocolic vessels; encircle superiorly.
- Careful blunt sweeping to visualize right ureter and duodenum.

## Right Colectomy: Vascular Ligation
- Once ureter and duodenum are safely visualized and out of the field.
- High ligation of the ileocolic vessel using hemolock clips, energy device, or vascular stapler.
- Medial-to-lateral dissection continues, dividing retroperitoneal attachments.
- Stay in appropriate retroperitoneal plane anterior to duodenum.

## Right Colectomy: Proximal Dissection
- Distal extent near falciform ligament or middle colic vessels.
- Hepatic flexure or proximal transverse tumors: further distal dissection to include middle colic vessels.
- Care in retroperitoneal space to avoid hemorrhage from pancreaticoduodenal and gastroepiploic veins.
- Right branch of middle colic divided if necessary.

## Right Colectomy: Lateral Attachments
- Right colon held only by lateral avascular attachments, hepatic flexure, and gastrocolic attachments.
- Divided using dissecting energy devices.
- Dissection carried distally to proximally.
- Gastrocolic attachments to transverse colon divided, often entering lesser sac.

## Right Colectomy: Hepatic Flexure Tumors
- Challenging due to surrounding anatomy (duodenum, pancreas, gallbladder, kidney).
- Omentum may be involved; must remain attached for en bloc resection.
- Entry into lesser sac helpful if retroperitoneal structures potentially involved.
- Dissect open gastrocolic ligament superior to transverse colon attachments.

## Right Colectomy: Extraction Site
- Once dissected, right colon mobilized and expressed as midline structure.
- Division and anastomosis performed intracorporeally or extracorporeally.
- Extraction site based on surgeon preference.
- Off-midline (e.g., Pfannenstiel) has lower rates of wound disruption, SSI, and complications compared to midline.
- Re-laparoscope to confirm hemostasis; perform TAP blocks.

## Notes on CME for Right Colectomy
- Dissection same as standard, but vessels ligated at origin.
- Trace ileocolic vessels to SMV, clearing tissue anterior and lateral to SMV.
- Follow plane to trunk of Henle (confluence of right gastroepiploic and superior right colic veins).
- Middle colic vessels appreciated; right branch ligated for ascending, hepatic, or proximal transverse cancers.
- Omentectomy en bloc usually performed.

## Transverse Colectomy and Middle Colic Vessels
- Transverse colon cancers are uncommon (10 percent).
- Proximal or mid tumors: extended right colectomy or isolated transverse colectomy.
- Regardless of operation, middle colic vessel must be ligated at origin.
- Challenging due to truncated length.
- Isolated by retracting transverse mesentery superiorly; window created and divided retrograde.

## Approach to Splenic Flexure Cancer
- Account for 3 to 5 percent of colon cancers; often present late with worse prognosis.
- Optimal operation debated: extended resection versus left colectomy.
- Extended resection: higher lymph node yield, but uncertain oncologic advantage and worse bowel function.
- Left colectomy: registry studies confirm it is oncologically safe, no survival difference, shorter operative time, quicker recovery.

## Left Colectomy: Positioning and Setup
- Resection of descending and/or splenic flexure.
- Anastomosis of distal transverse colon to sigmoid colon.
- Modified lithotomy or split-leg position; both arms tucked.
- Allows option for intraoperative colonoscopy (useful if tumor not tattooed).
- Head down, left side raised.

## Left Colectomy: Medial-to-Lateral Steps
- Identify duodenojejunal flexure to locate inferior mesenteric vein (IMV).
- Sub-IMV approach: stay posterior to IMV, ligate IMV just below pancreas.
- Continue plane laterally, freeing left mesocolon from retroperitoneum.
- Transmesenteric approach into lesser sac anterior to peripancreatic fat.

## Left Colectomy: Vascular Ligation
- Identify IMA through mesocolic fascia.
- Open infra-IMA plane to identify IMA at origin.
- Identify left colic artery and take high at origin, preserving IMA.
- Patient placed head up; follow transmesenteric window to ligate left branch of middle colic vessels.
- Open gastrocolic omentum close to stomach; take omentum en bloc.

## Sigmoid Colectomy: Positioning and Setup
- Modified lithotomy or split-leg position.
- Right arm tucked (lap), both arms tucked (robotic).
- Same port placements as left colectomy.
- Head down, left side raised.

## Sigmoid Colectomy: Lateral-to-Medial Approach
- Release lateral attachments of sigmoid and left colon from abdominal wall.
- Dissection plane 1 to 2 mm medial to lateral retroperitoneal attachments.
- Imperative to identify left ureter (easiest at apex of sigmoid mesocolon).
- Continue to medialize sigmoid, staying anterior to Gerota fascia.

## Sigmoid Colectomy: Splenic Flexure Mobilization
- Develop retrorectal plane posterior to upper rectum.
- Patient placed head up; enter lesser sac above transverse colon.
- Mobilize splenic flexure by dissecting phrenocolic and splenocolic attachments.
- Avoid excess traction on spleen.
- Release transverse mesocolon from inferior border of pancreas to join previous dissection plane.

## Sigmoid Colectomy: Vascular Ligation and Transection
- Develop plane posterior to IMA, preserving hypogastric autonomic nervous plexus.
- Ligate IMA near origin (proximal to left colic artery) for nodal harvest.
- Ligate IMV if needed for conduit length.
- Mobilize upper rectum circumferentially; divide rectum with endoscopic stapler.
- Evaluate proximal colon vascularity (Parks test, ICG fluorescence).

## Total Abdominal Colectomy: Positioning and Ports
- Modified lithotomy; both arms tucked.
- Requires 6-port technique for laparoscopic or robotic.
- Extraction site through midline or Pfannenstiel.
- Reference Figure 182.11 for port configurations.

## Total Abdominal Colectomy: Right and Transverse Dissection
- Begin at transverse colon; dissect omentum off.
- Mobilize transverse colon from gastrocolic ligament.
- Visualize and ligate middle colic pedicle near SMA origin.
- Carry dissection to hepatic flexure; free from retroperitoneum (protect duodenum and pancreas).
- Divide lateral attachments; high ligation of ileocolic and right colic vessels.

## Total Abdominal Colectomy: Left Dissection
- Tilt patient right side down, Trendelenburg.
- Dissect transverse mesentery from retroperitoneum toward splenic flexure.
- Separate omentum from transverse colon to enter lesser sac.
- Pull descending colon medially; sweep pericolonic tissues from retroperitoneum.
- Mobilize left colon as far superiorly as possible in posterior mesenteric plane.

## Total Abdominal Colectomy: IMA and Extraction
- Incise peritoneum right of IMA near sacral promontory.
- Identify and preserve hypogastric nervous plexus.
- Identify and sweep left ureter and gonadal vessels posteriorly.
- Ligate IMA with clips and energy device.
- Transect rectosigmoid junction with stapler.
- Extract specimen; fashion end ileostomy or perform ileorectal anastomosis.

## Review: Table 182.1 (Short-Term Outcomes)
- Summarizes operative time, LOS, complications, mortality, conversion, and lymph node harvest.
- Laparoscopic consistently shows longer operative time but shorter LOS.
- Conversion rates vary (3 to 25 percent) but decrease with experience.
- Morbidity and mortality generally equivalent or lower for MIS.
- Lymph node harvest equivalent or better with MIS.

## Review: Table 182.2 (Return of Bowel Function)
- Compares time to flatus, bowel movement, PO tolerance, and length of ileus.
- Laparoscopic consistently shows earlier return of bowel function compared to open.
- Time to flatus often 1 to 2 days earlier.
- Robotic approaches show similar or slightly improved times compared to laparoscopic.

## Review: Table 182.3 (Postoperative Pain Control)
- Measures days of parenteral narcotics, oral analgesics, and visual analog scales.
- Laparoscopic requires fewer days of parenteral and oral analgesics compared to open.
- Visual analog scale scores significantly lower for laparoscopic on Postoperative Day 1.
- Robotic and laparoscopic pain scores are generally comparable.

## Review: Table 182.4 (Long-Term Outcomes)
- Summarizes overall survival, disease-free survival, wound recurrence, incisional hernia, and SBO.
- Major trials (COST, CLASICC, COLOR) show NO difference in survival or recurrence between open and lap.
- LAFA study showed decreased incisional hernia and SBO in laparoscopic group.
- Long-term oncologic equivalence is firmly established.

## Figure 182.1: Port Placements
- Illustrates 4-port technique for laparoscopic right colectomy.
- Illustrates 4-arm technique for robotic right colectomy (da Vinci Xi).
- Camera and assistant ports strategically placed for optimal triangulation.
- Extraction site through midline or surgeon preference.

## Figure 182.2: The Bowstring Effect
- Demonstrates grasping the cecum or mesentery and lifting anterolaterally.
- Creates a tenting or bowstring effect.
- Highlights the ileocolic artery branching off the SMA.
- Distinct crease courses parallel to the vessel, guiding dissection.

## Figure 182.3: Medial-to-Lateral Mobilization
- Highlights the duodenum and the white line of Toldt.
- Demonstrates the retroperitoneal plane.
- Crucial for visualizing and protecting the duodenum during right colectomy.

## Figures 182.4 and 182.5: Hepatic Flexure and Lesser Sac
- Figure 182.4: Hepatic flexure tumor involving right kidney and duodenum.
- Figure 182.5: Accessing the lesser sac through the omentum (gastrocolic ligament).
- Early entry into the lesser sac is key to facilitating mobilization of the transverse colon.

## Figure 182.6: Middle Colic Vessel Anatomy
- Classic Y pattern is not always straightforward.
- Often both right and left branches course to the patient's right.
- Right branch courses off the head of the pancreas and duodenum.
- Left branch makes a sharp upward turn and veers left.

## Figures 182.7 to 182.10: Left and Sigmoid Anatomy
- Figure 182.7: Port placements for left and sigmoid colectomy.
- Figure 182.8: The critical angle between IMA and sacral promontory marks the avascular plane.
- Figure 182.9: Care taken to identify and avoid left ureter, gonadal vessels, and hypogastric nerves.
- Figure 182.10: Mobilization between IMA and IMV facilitates splenic flexure mobilization.

## Conclusion
- Ongoing evidence supports feasibility and safety of MIS for colon cancer.
- Laparoscopy remains most widely used; robotics gaining momentum.
- MIS is a tool to successfully remove pathology.
- Must ensure equivalent operation regarding patient safety and oncologic outcome compared to open approach.
